“Hear me, then! You!” answered Monks. “His father having fallen ill in Rome, his wife, my mother, from whom he had long been separated, came to him from Paris, bringing me along—to look after his fortune, for aught I know, since she had little love for him, and he as little for her. He did not recognize us, having lost his senses, and slept on until the following day, when he died. In his desk, among his papers, were two dated the night he was first taken ill, and addressed to you”; he turned to Mr. Brownlow; “enclosed with a few brief lines for you, and a direction upon the wrapper that the packet should not be sent until his death. One paper was a letter to this girl Agnes; the other was a will.”

“And the letter?” Mr. Brownlow asked.

“The letter?—A page written across and across again, full of penitent confession and prayers that God would aid her. He had imposed upon the girl a story that some hidden mystery—to be made plain one day—kept him from marrying her at present; and thus she had continued, patiently believing him, till her trust went too far, and she lost what nobody could restore. At that time she was within a few months of her confinement. He explained everything he had intended to do, had he lived, to conceal her shame, and begged her, if he died, neither to curse his remembrance nor suppose that the punishment of their sin would fall on her or their little child; the whole guilt belonged to him. He recalled the day when he gave her the small locket and the ring engraved with her christian name, with a space remaining for the name he hoped to give her some day—begged her still to preserve it, and wear it beside her heart as she used to do—and then wandered wildly on, repeating the same expressions again and again, as though he had lost his reason. I believe he had.”

“The will,” Mr. Brownlow said, while Oliver's tears flowed quickly.

Monks said nothing.

“The will,” continued Mr. Brownlow, answering for him, “was written in the same spirit as the letter. He spoke of the wretchedness his wife had inflicted upon him; of the rebellious temper, wickedness, malice, and early evil passions of you, his only son, brought up to hate him; and bequeathed to you and your mother an annuity of eight hundred pounds apiece. The greater part of his fortune he separated into two equal shares—one belonging to Agnes Fleming, the other to their child, provided it was born alive and should attain its majority.”

Sir Walter had rented a very fine house in Camden Place, in a high and distinguished location suited to a man of importance; and he and Elizabeth had settled there to their considerable satisfaction.

Anne entered with a heavy heart, expecting to feel imprisoned for many months, and anxiously thinking, “Oh, when will I leave you again?” The unexpected warmth of her reception, however, lifted her spirits. Her father and sister were pleased to see her because they could show her the house and its furniture, and they greeted her kindly. When they sat down to dinner, they remarked on the benefit of having a fourth person at the table.

Mrs Clay was very agreeable and all smiles, but her politeness and smiles were more predictable. Anne had always expected her to put on the proper show when she arrived; the friendliness of the others came as a surprise. They were clearly in excellent spirits, and she would soon hear why. They had no desire to hear her news. After fishing for assurances that everyone in their former neighbourhood missed them terribly, which Anne could not give, they asked only a few halfhearted questions before taking over the conversation entirely. Uppercross interested them not at all, and Kellynch very little: everything was about Bath.

They were delighted to assure her that Bath had exceeded their expectations in every way. Their house was unquestionably the best in Camden Place; their drawing rooms had several clear advantages over all the others they had seen or heard about, and the quality of the decoration and the taste shown in the furniture were equally superior. Their company was in enormous demand. Everyone wanted to visit them. They had declined numerous introductions, yet people they knew nothing about were still constantly leaving calling cards.

Here was plenty to enjoy. Could Anne be surprised that her father and sister were happy? She could hardly be surprised, but she had to sigh that her father felt no loss of standing in his altered circumstances, regretted none of the responsibilities and dignity of living on his own estate, and found so much to flatter his vanity in the trivialities of town life. And she had to sigh, and smile, and marvel too, as Elizabeth flung open the folding doors and walked triumphantly from one drawing room to the other, boasting of their spaciousness: how could a woman who had presided over Kellynch Hall take pride in the distance between two walls perhaps thirty feet apart?

But these were not their only reasons for happiness. They had Mr Elliot as well.

The following day was fixed for producing the evidence (lest delay should give our honour a chill), and on that day Drummle arrived with a courteously worded little acknowledgment in Estella's handwriting, declaring that she had enjoyed the honour of dancing with him on several occasions. There remained nothing for me but to express regret at having been “led into a warmth which,” and generally to abandon as indefensible the assertion that I was to be found anywhere. Drummle and I then spent an hour snorting at each other, while the Grove contradicted everybody without distinction; after which it was pronounced that good feeling had advanced at an astonishing pace.

I relate it lightly, but to me it was far from a light affair. I cannot properly convey the suffering I felt at the thought that Estella could bestow any favour upon a despicable, awkward, sullen dolt, so much beneath the ordinary level. Even now, I believe some genuine flame of generosity and unselfishness in my love for her made the notion of her lowering herself to that cur intolerable to me. Doubtless I should have suffered whoever received her favour; but a more deserving object would have brought a different measure and species of pain.

It was not difficult to discover, and I soon discovered, that Drummle had started attending her closely, and that she permitted his attentions. Before long, he pursued her everywhere, and he and I encountered one another daily. He persisted with a stupid doggedness, and Estella kept him persisting; sometimes encouraging, sometimes repulsing him, at one moment nearly flattering him, at another showing him open contempt, now treating him as an intimate, now barely recalling who he was.

The Spider, as Mr. Jaggers had named him, was accustomed to waiting in ambush, however, and possessed the patience of his kind. Besides this, he had a dullard's faith in his wealth and the grandeur of his family, which occasionally served him well—almost supplying the place of concentrated attention and resolution. Thus the Spider, stubbornly keeping his eyes upon Estella, outwaited many livelier insects, and would frequently uncoil himself and descend at precisely the proper moment.

At an Assembly Ball in Richmond (Assembly Balls were then held in most places), where Estella eclipsed every other beauty, this lumbering Drummle hovered about her so constantly, and was so readily tolerated, that I determined to speak to her about him. I seized the first chance that offered: she was waiting for Mrs. Blandley to take her home, seated by herself among some flowers and prepared to depart.
